sections.h2: Which notice does a Kansas landlord have to give first?
sections.html:
It depends on why the landlord wants the tenant out. The Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act sets different written notices for unpaid rent, for a lease violation and for ending a periodic tenancy, and each one has its own wording requirements.

SituationNotice periodStatute
Unpaid rent3 days (three consecutive 24 hour periods)K.S.A. 58-2564(b)
Material lease violationTermination at least 30 days after receipt if not fixed within 14 daysK.S.A. 58-2564(a)
Repeat of a similar breach30 days, with no chance to cureK.S.A. 58-2564(a)
Month-to-month tenancy30 days, ending on a rent-paying dateK.S.A. 58-2570(b)
Week-to-week tenancy7 days before the termination dateK.S.A. 58-2570(a)

All of these notices are in writing. The text of each section is on the Kansas Legislature's site, for example K.S.A. 58-2564.

sections.h2: How are the three days for unpaid rent counted in Kansas?
sections.html:
The clock starts when the notice is delivered or posted, and it runs as three full 24 hour periods. K.S.A. 58-2564(b) says that if the notice is served on the tenant or on a person over 12 years of age living on the premises, or posted in a conspicuous place on the premises, the period begins at delivery or posting.

If the notice goes by mail, the statute allows an additional two days from the date of mailing. The notice must state that rent is unpaid and that the landlord intends to end the rental agreement if it is not paid within the three days. Read the statute before drafting, because those two statements are part of what the notice has to say.

If the tenant pays the full rent within the period, the termination does not take effect. A landlord who is unsure how the notice was served should keep a record of the date, the time and the method used, since the three days are counted from that moment.

sections.h2: What about a lease violation or an expired lease?
sections.html:
For a material breach, the landlord delivers a notice that lists the acts or omissions and says the agreement will end on a date at least 30 days after receipt if the breach is not remedied in 14 days. If the problem can be fixed by repairs or payment and the tenant makes a good faith effort before the date in the notice, the agreement does not terminate.

When the same or a similar breach recurs after the 14 days, the landlord may serve a new 30 day notice that gives no chance to cure. The agreement then ends as the notice says, regardless of the periodic rent-paying date.

A tenant who stays after the lease term ends, or after termination, without the landlord's consent is a holdover. Under K.S.A. 58-2570(c) the landlord may bring an action for possession. If the holdover is willful and not in good faith, the landlord may recover up to 1.5 months' periodic rent or up to 1.5 times actual damages, whichever is greater. A tenant in the military who needs to end a month-to-month tenancy because of orders needs to give no more than 15 days' written notice.

sections.h2: What happens in court after the notice period ends?
sections.html:
The landlord files an eviction petition, and K.S.A. 61-3801 through 61-3808 govern those lawsuits. The Kansas Judicial Branch's self-help site gives a typical timeline of up to 42 days from petition to the end of the process.

  • Step 1: the landlord files a petition. The hearing is scheduled within 3 to 14 days.
  • Step 2: the court issues a summons. The tenant must respond in writing or appear at the hearing, or a default judgment can be entered.
  • Step 3: if the tenant responds and disagrees, a bench trial is set within 14 days of the hearing date.
  • Step 4: the judge rules.
  • Step 5: if the landlord wins, a writ of restitution issues and is executed within 14 days.

Service of the summons in a forcible detainer case must be returned no later than three days before the date set for the tenant to appear or plead (K.S.A. 61-3005). The Kansas Judicial Council posts forms and instructions for both landlords and tenants.

sections.h2: Who can carry out the eviction in Kansas?
sections.html:
Only the person named in the writ of restitution, who must be someone authorized to serve process. The statute names no other route for removal after judgment.

K.S.A. 61-3808 says the writ must be executed within 14 days after the named person receives it, and that person may use reasonable force as needed. If the tenant appeals and the court stays the proceedings, the officer must stop at once, and if the tenant has already been removed, the tenant is restored to the home.

There is also a faster option in some cases. K.S.A. 58-2570(d) lets a landlord ask for an order of immediate possession during an action for possession. The judge must be satisfied that it is in the interest of justice, and can require the landlord to post an undertaking to cover the tenant's damages if the tenant wins.

sections.h2: What new Kansas eviction record rules apply in 2026?
sections.html:
Starting July 1, 2026, some eviction cases in Kansas can be expunged, which removes the court record from public view. The Kansas Judicial Branch runs an online Eviction Expungement Portal for people who represent themselves, and the change comes from 2026 Substitute for House Bill 2357.

For a landlord, this means a former tenant may later ask a court to expunge a case, and the landlord may object using the form provided. For a seller, it is a reason to keep copies of the notice, the petition and any judgment in your own files, since the public record may not always be there to prove what happened.

sections.h2: How does an eviction affect selling a Kansas rental house?
sections.html:
A house with a tenant in a dispute is harder to sell on the open market, because buyers who plan to live in it expect possession at closing. The notices above only work if they are accurate, delivered correctly and followed by the court steps, which can take up to 42 days even when nothing goes wrong.

Some counties run programs that can help both sides settle first. The Kansas self-help site lists the Johnson County District Court's Eviction Mediation Program, the Douglas County Eviction Resolution Program and the Sedgwick County Eviction Resolution Program, which connect landlords and tenants with information, mediation and rental assistance.

  • Kansas Legal Services publishes a Landlord Handbook and a tenant rights guide.
  • The Kansas Housing Resource Corporation and 211 Kansas list rental help and emergency shelter.
  • Ask a Kansas attorney whether an existing lease continues after a sale of the house, since the answer depends on the lease terms.

faqs.q: How many days notice is required to evict for nonpayment in Kansas?
faqs.a: Three days, counted as three consecutive 24 hour periods after delivery or posting, with two extra days if the notice is mailed (K.S.A. 58-2564(b)).

faqs.q: How much notice ends a month-to-month tenancy in Kansas?
faqs.a: At least 30 days after receipt, ending on a rent-paying date. A tenant in the military with orders can give no more than 15 days (K.S.A. 58-2570(b)).

faqs.q: How long does a Kansas eviction take after the notice?
faqs.a: The Kansas Judicial Branch says the court process can take up to 42 days. A hearing is set 3 to 14 days after the petition, and a writ must be executed within 14 days.

faqs.q: Can a landlord remove a tenant without a court order?
faqs.a: No. Removal is done by the person named in the writ of restitution, under K.S.A. 61-3808, after a judgment for possession.

faqs.q: Can an eviction case be removed from the record in Kansas?
faqs.a: Starting July 1, 2026, some eviction cases can be expunged through a court motion. The Judicial Branch offers an online portal for self-represented people.
